pages.text: Common glass is soda-lime: sand, soda and lime. Heat one side and that side swells while the rest does not, and it cracks.
pages.title: Borosilicate

pages.text: Otto Schott at Jena found in the 1890s that boric oxide in place of most of the soda and lime made a glass that expands a third as much, and Corning sold it from 1915 as Pyrex: four fifths silica, an eighth boric oxide, a little soda and alumina. It goes from a flame into cold water and holds.

Borax is sodium borate, so it brings the boron and the soda both. Three colourless sand and a raw borax, superheated, melt to three borosilicate glass; it wants more heat than soda-lime, which melts in any furnace. Six make sixteen panes.
It is no stronger than glass, and shatters as glass does unless it is lifted with silk touch.

Its job here is the hottest one. High-level waste from PUREX is melted with borosilicate glass, superheated, into vitrified waste: boron and silica take the fission products into the glass's own network, which is how every vitrification plant locks them up.
pages.title: Vitrification
